extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (patent agents and attorneys), USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline stakeholders, and respondents in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and remedial measures governing conduct of practitioners before the USPTO, especially relating to use of Customer Numbers, duties of competence and diligence, signature/filing requirements, and disciplinary sanctions. The document is a USPTO Final Order that both finds violations of specific professional conduct rules and prescribes sanctions and practice-improvement measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.101 (competence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner must have competence; violations include not understanding that, by being appointed as a co-practitioner of record via Customer Number practice, she could become the sole practitioner of record and not knowing or understanding that by using USPTO electronic databases she could identify customer numbers from which another practitioner was removed and each application on which she was sole practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes: (i) understanding that appointment via Customer Number can result in becoming sole practitioner on applications the practitioner may not otherwise know about; and (ii) knowing how to use USPTO electronic databases to identify each Customer Number from which another registered practitioner had been removed and each patent application on which the practitioner is sole practitioner. Practitioners should proactively learn and understand USPTO processes (e.g., Customer Number implications) and relevant electronic tools (searching USPTO databases) to maintain competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 (diligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with diligence in handling client patent matters. The Order finds failure of diligence where a practitioner (inter alia) allowed a non-practitioner/company to appoint her as co-practitioner on thousands of applications without knowledge of the other practitioner; did not know on what applications she had been appointed; did not timely learn when the other practitioner had been removed; and was not aware of the risk of harm to client rights and to the patent process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence obligations include: (i) knowing which matters you are the practitioner of record for; (ii) timely monitoring changes (e.g., removals of co-practitioners) that affect your status; (iii) recognizing and acting upon risks to client IP rights and the integrity of the patent process; and (iv) avoiding business arrangements that leave practitioners unaware of what applications they are appointed to handle. Anti-patterns: passively accepting appointment via Customer Number and failing to monitor docket activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d) (conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the USPTO patent application process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that prejudices the integrity of the USPTO process includes failing to appreciate that Customer Number appointment can make one the sole practitioner of record, not using USPTO databases to identify Customer Numbers and sole-practitioner matters, allowing non-practitioners to appoint the practitioner as co-practitioner on thousands of matters without knowledge/communication with co-practitioners, failing to know on which applications one is appointed, and not timely learning removals — conduct that in this matter culminated in becoming the only practitioner on 146 applications where responses were filed signed by an officer/manager rather than a registered practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must avoid conduct that undermines the integrity of the patent application process. Examples of prejudicial conduct include enabling non-practitioners to control appointments, failing to monitor practitioner status, and permitting filings that are not prepared or reviewed by registered practitioners. The presence of filings signed by non-registered officers (see 37 C.F.R. § 1.33(b)(3)) is an indicium of prejudice to the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 1.33(b)(3) (signature/preparation requirement for filings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to Show Cause Orders were filed in some applications that were signed by an officer or manager of a juristic entity applicant, instead of a registered patent practitioner, in violation of 37 C.F.R. § 1.33(b)(3); such responses were seemingly not prepared or reviewed by a registered practitioner prior to filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that filings required to be made by or through registered practitioners are in fact reviewed and signed by a registered practitioner as required. Do not permit or rely on filings signed solely by non-registered officers/managers where PTO rules require practitioner preparation/review. Anti-pattern: allowing or ignoring filings by non-practitioners that should be practitioner-reviewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Customer Number practice and MPEP §403 (proper use and oversight of Customer Numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Order references MPEP § 403 concerning Customer Numbers and highlights risks where third parties use Customer Numbers to appoint registered practitioners as practitioners or co-practitioners on applications without the practitioner knowing the specific matters involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must understand the Customer Number mechanism (see MPEP §403), and the potential for third-party assignment. Guidance includes using USPTO databases to identify which Customer Numbers and applications you are associated with, and treating Customer Number appointments with caution. Consider docket controls that avoid reliance on third-party Customer Numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice safeguards when associated with Customer Numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent agreed to adopt practice changes to ensure future conduct comports with ethical standards: (a) reasonably seek to avoid being associated with a customer number to which another practitioner with whom respondent does not have a close business relationship is also associated; (b) reasonably remain in contact with other practitioners who are associated with customer numbers with which respondent is also associated; (c) reasonably and closely monitor activity on any matters associated with a customer number with which respondent is also associated; and (d) always consider using alternative docket control measures that, unlike customer numbers, do not allow third parties to be associated with patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four measures are concrete best practices: avoid shared Customer Numbers with unknown practitioners; maintain communication with co-practitioners; actively monitor docket activity on Customer Number matters; and adopt independent docket-control systems (e.g., firm-specific dockets) that prevent third-party appointment. These are practical steps to prevent the anti-patterns that led to disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.504 (professional independence when entering business relationships)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must preserve professional independence when entering into business relationships where a non-practitioner or non-practitioner entity refers work to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fee-sharing or referral arrangements or business relationships that would impair independence or enable non-practitioners to control practice before the USPTO. Scrutinize arrangements with non-practitioner entities that refer work and ensure independence and compliance with ethical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.505 (assisting in unauthorized practice of law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not assist in the unauthorized practice of law by non-practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not facilitate or enable non-registered persons or entities to perform tasks that amount to practice before the USPTO that require a registered practitioner. Monitor submissions and filings to ensure they are properly prepared/reviewed by registered practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104 (communications with clients)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must communicate with clients about the patent and trademark matters for which the practitioner is the practitioner of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain effective client communications: confirm authority before filing on a client's behalf, obtain express instructions when required, and keep clients informed about their matters. Anti-pattern: filing responses without express client authorization when required or failing to confirm who has authority to instruct filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.107 (conflicts of interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must be mindful of conflicts of interest implicated under circumstances like those presented where third parties appoint practitioners by Customer Number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and manage conflicts when accepting work via Customer Numbers or third-party referrals; ensure duties to clients are not compromised by business relationships or associations with unknown co-practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.116 (declining or terminating representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are obligations regarding declining or terminating representation; practitioners should follow applicable rules when withdrawing or continuing representation in matters assigned via Customer Numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When authority or appropriate instructions are absent, consider whether to withdraw; adhere to procedural and ethical requirements for terminating representation so clients' interests are protected (e.g., avoid filing responses without express authority when necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i) (other conduct adversely reflecting on fitness to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must avoid other conduct that adversely reflects on their fitness to practice before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain professional conduct that does not undermine public confidence in the practitioner’s fitness to practice. Avoid patterns of behavior (e.g., poor oversight of filings, enabling non-practitioner control) that could be characterized as adverse to fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation with USPTO investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent shall cooperate fully with the USPTO in any present or future inquiry into any person or third-party entities, including persons or entities reasonably believed to have been involved in preparing, signing, filing, or arranging filings in the relevant matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subject to inquiry, provide full cooperation (documents, interviews, information about third parties). Cooperation is an important remedial factor and may be expected as part of settlements or probation terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing education and remedial training
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent certified viewing the USPTO recording 'Patent Priorities for FY2025 and Fraud and Threat Mitigation' and reviewed applicable MPEP provisions and general ethics course materials (e.g., Ethical Issues in Business and the Lawyer's Role).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should undertake continuing education on USPTO priorities, fraud mitigation, MPEP provisions (including MPEP §403 on Customer Numbers), and ethics resources to maintain competence and avoid ethical lapses. Such training and review can be mitigating in disciplinary contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and enforcement procedures (reprimand, probation, show-cause, suspension, publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreed-upon sanctions in this matter include a public reprimand; probation for twelve months; procedures empowering the OED Director to issue an Order to Show Cause and to seek immediate suspension of up to 90 days if the practitioner fails to comply during probation; rights to respond to show-cause orders (15 days); and publication of the Final Order in the OED FOIA Reading Room and the Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences for violations can include public reprimand, probation, and suspension. The enforcement process includes issuance of an Order to Show Cause, notice to the practitioner, a 15-day response window, possible submission to the USPTO Director requesting suspension, and publication of disciplinary results. A practitioner on probation should comply strictly with all terms to avoid expedited suspension; review settlement terms carefully (e.g., waivers of appeal or review may be included).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice requirements for disciplinary actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order at the OED FOIA Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the provided Notice of Reprimand and Probation, describing the violations and the misconduct's implications for practitioners generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary outcomes are made public; practitioners should be aware that records of proceedings may be used by the Office in future matters and will be accessible publicly. This underscores the reputational consequences of disciplinary findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement terms and potential future use of proceeding record
rubrics_metrics.description: The Final Order notes the action is the result of a settlement agreement and provides that the Office may consider the record of this disciplinary proceeding in future complaints or proceedings concerning the same or similar misconduct — as an aggravating factor or to rebut representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement may include waivers (e.g., rights to reconsideration or review) and does not preclude the Office from using the record in future disciplinary contexts. Practitioners should understand that settlement terms may have lasting effects and the record may impact future discipline.
